reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: A sclerosing bone dysplasia combining progressive craniofacial hyperostosis with abnormal metaphyseal modelling of the long bones
The autosomal dominant form is caused by mutations in ANKH; a rarer autosomal recessive form is linked to GJA1
Facial features include a broad nasal bridge, paranasal bossing and hypertelorism that progress with age
Cranial nerve compression from thickened skull base bone can cause facial palsy, hearing loss and, less often, visual impairment
Nasal airway obstruction and choanal narrowing may occur from hyperostosis of the facial bones
Radiographs show a widened, club-shaped or 'Erlenmeyer flask' metaphyseal deformity of the long bones alongside diffuse cranial sclerosis
It must be distinguished from craniodiaphyseal dysplasia, which is far more severe with predominantly diaphyseal involvement
Management is largely supportive with surgical decompression of foramina considered for symptomatic cranial nerve compression
reference.pathophysiology: Craniometaphyseal dysplasia is a disorder of bone modelling. The dominant form results from mutations in ANKH, a transmembrane protein that transports inorganic pyrophosphate, a key inhibitor of mineralisation, out of cells; disturbed pyrophosphate handling alters the balance of bone deposition and resorption. The consequence is excessive, poorly remodelled bone in the skull and face (hyperostosis and sclerosis) together with defective tubulation of the long-bone metaphyses. The recessive form involves the gap-junction protein connexin 43 encoded by GJA1. Progressive skull-base thickening narrows the neural foramina and causes the cranial neuropathies.
additionalDifferentials: Pyle disease (metaphyseal dysplasia with mild skull change)
Van Buchem disease and sclerosteosis (SOST-related sclerosis)
Fibrous dysplasia of the craniofacial bones
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing of ANKH (and GJA1 for suspected recessive disease)
Skull and facial radiographs or CT to document hyperostosis and foraminal narrowing
Long-bone radiographs to demonstrate metaphyseal flaring
Audiological assessment for conductive and sensorineural hearing loss
Cranial nerve examination and imaging of the skull base foramina
Ophthalmological and nasal airway assessment where symptoms suggest compression
redFlags: Progressive facial nerve palsy or hearing loss from foraminal narrowing
Visual deterioration suggesting optic nerve compression
Significant nasal airway obstruction from facial hyperostosis
Rapid clinical progression raising concern for craniodiaphyseal dysplasia
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is usually normal, but the craniofacial changes are progressive and cranial nerve compression can cause lasting facial weakness, hearing loss or visual problems, so long-term surveillance and timely surgical decompression are important.
pitfalls: Confusing it with the much more severe craniodiaphyseal dysplasia, altering prognosis
Attributing hearing loss solely to middle-ear disease and missing bony foraminal compression
Delaying decompression until cranial nerve deficits become irreversible
Overlooking the metaphyseal long-bone changes that support the diagnosis
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Supportive and surgical management, as no medical therapy reverses the excessive craniofacial bone deposition
Surgical decompression of narrowed skull-base foramina to relieve compression of the facial, auditory and optic nerves
Audiological assessment with hearing aids for conductive and sensorineural hearing loss
Ophthalmological monitoring for optic nerve compromise
Management of nasal airway and choanal obstruction arising from facial hyperostosis
Regular cranial-nerve surveillance with imaging of the skull-base foramina
Multidisciplinary care with genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant ANKH form and the rarer autosomal recessive GJA1 form
